title: Acme Fintech x Redwood — Optimize Guardrails + Eval Gating Technical Deep Dive
customer_attendees: Tom Becker (Engineering Manager, Customer Support AI)
next_steps: Acme to share a redacted prompt set + expected outputs (or rubric) for two workflows: support-agent drafting and policy Q&A.
Redwood to send the Guardrails pilot plan: gating stages (observe-only → soft-block → hard-block), suggested metrics, and minimum sample size defaults.
Redwood to provide audit log event examples for OptimizeConfigChange (pass/fail reasons, suite versions, override fields) and retention defaults.
Schedule a 60-min pilot kickoff + prompt-set onboarding session (Acme ML Platform + Redwood Evals/Platform).
Security follow-up: Redwood to send SOC 2 report + data retention/PII handling note for eval artifacts; Acme to send vendor security questionnaire.
action_items: Miguel Santos (Redwood) - Send pilot kickoff email with proposed timeline and required inputs (prompt sets, success criteria) - Due 2025-01-16
Olivia Grant (Redwood) - Share technical doc links: gating output format, suite selector by optimization type, and timeout/ retry behavior - Due 2025-01-17
Jonas Weber (Redwood) - Propose initial threshold defaults for Acme’s two workflows (task success + format adherence + toxicity) incl. minimum sample sizes - Due 2025-01-21
Ethan Park (Redwood) - Confirm override RBAC + audit fields and whether Acme can require 2-person approval for overrides - Due 2025-01-21
Sarah Kim (Acme) - Provide 50–100 representative prompts per workflow + scoring guidance (rubric or expected JSON schema) - Due 2025-01-24

summary: Acme Fintech asked for a technical deep dive on Redwood Optimize and the upcoming Quality Guardrails “gating” that blocks (or requires override for) cost-saving config changes when quality risks are detected. Discussion focused on: (1) what changes Optimize may apply (quantization, batching, caching, routing), (2) how gating runs targeted eval suites with model/version + prompt-set revision pinning, (3) threshold schema (per metric/workload/model family) including minimum sample sizes and confidence rules, (4) timeout/failure behavior and safe-degrade, (5) audit logging/override RBAC for regulated workflows. Acme’s main concerns: avoiding silent quality regressions in customer-facing support drafts, proving checks ran (audit evidence), and having a controlled override path during incidents.
topics: Optimize config deltas that can affect output quality (quantization, caching/batching, routing/fallback)
Eval harness integration: suite selection, outputs, confidence intervals, minimum sample sizes
Prompt-set requirements and coverage for tool calling / structured output
Threshold schema/versioning: pinning to model + prompt-set revision
Operational concerns: timeouts, flaky graders, reruns, and rollout stages
Audit logs, retention, and RBAC for overrides
questions: Can we require gating for any quantization change, but allow batching changes to proceed with a soft-block during pilot?
If the eval runner is down, do we always block applies, or can we allow manual approval for our enterprise tier with full auditing?
Can thresholds be different for ‘support draft’ vs ‘policy Q&A’ even if it’s the same model?
Do you store our prompts/outputs, and what’s the retention policy for eval artifacts?
What’s the mechanism for proving to auditors that a specific config change had passing evals at the time it was applied?
transcript:
Meeting: Acme Fintech x Redwood — Optimize Guardrails + Eval Gating Technical Deep Dive
Recorded: 2025-01-14 18:05 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood: Miguel Santos (AE), Olivia Grant (Solutions/SE), Jonas Weber (Applied ML / Evals), Ethan Park (Platform Control Plane)
- Acme Fintech: Sarah Kim (ML Platform), Anil Mehta (Staff ML Eng), Rachel Owens (Security/GRC), Tom Becker (Eng Mgr)

---

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone. Goal today is to go deep on Optimize and specifically the guardrails gating work we mentioned last time—how it blocks or flags changes that might save cost but risk quality.

[00:16] Sarah Kim: Yep. For context, we got burned last quarter by what was effectively a “small” inference change and suddenly our support drafts got… more confident, less correct. So we’re trying to avoid the silent regression problem.

[00:30] Miguel Santos: Totally. That’s basically the exact class of issue driving the project. Olivia, do you want to set baseline of what Optimize can change today?

[00:38] Olivia Grant: Sure. So Optimize, at a high level, proposes configuration changes at serving time. Common ones are: enabling or adjusting continuous batching, toggling prefix/KV caching strategies, switching quantization profiles, and in some cases routing tweaks—like moving a route to a cheaper compatible variant, or changing fallback order.

[00:58] Anil Mehta: When you say quantization profiles, are you talking like int8, fp8, int4…?

[01:02] Olivia Grant: Yeah. Depending on model family and hardware, it can be FP8, INT8, INT4-ish variants. I’ll caveat: the exact profile names differ and sometimes the transcript will butcher them. But conceptually, it’s “more aggressive compression” to reduce cost.

[01:16] Tom Becker: And historically that’s the one that scares us the most, because it changes reasoning.

[01:22] Jonas Weber: That aligns with what we see. Quantization tends to introduce the most subtle quality shifts: format drift, missing fields in structured output, “reasoning got shorter,” tool-call arguments degrade. Batching/caching is usually safer but can still impact outputs via timing, truncation edge cases, or even nondeterminism if something isn’t pinned.

[01:45] Sarah Kim: So, what exactly is this “gating”? Like, is it a new product feature or internal thing?

[01:51] Miguel Santos: It’s part of Optimize. The idea is: any Optimize-driven apply is gated by eval checks. If it doesn’t meet thresholds, the apply is blocked by default—or during pilot, it can be soft-block with an override path.

[02:06] Ethan Park: And importantly, the enforcement point is in the control plane. So whether you’re clicking in the Console or calling the API, the same policy is evaluated, and we produce an auditable decision record.

[02:19] Rachel Owens: When you say auditable… that’s the part I care about. We need evidence of what was checked.

[02:26] Ethan Park: Right. For each apply attempt, we emit an audit event with: who initiated, what config delta, the eval suite ID(s), model version, prompt-set revision, pass/fail reasons, and any override info including justification.

[02:45] Rachel Owens: Okay. And is that exportable?

[02:48] Ethan Park: Yes, we support audit log export patterns. Specifics depend on your deployment mode, but generally you can stream to your SIEM or pull via API.

[03:00] Olivia Grant: Maybe we should walk through the flow from a developer standpoint. Then Jonas can go deeper on metrics and thresholds.

[03:07] Sarah Kim: Please.

[03:08] Olivia Grant: So, say Optimize recommends “move support-drafts route from quant profile Q1 to Q2,” or “increase max batch tokens,” etc. When you hit Apply, we create an apply request. That triggers a gating run: we select an eval suite based on optimization type plus tags on the workload—chat, tool calling, structured output, and also prompt length distribution if available.

[03:33] Anil Mehta: How do you know our workload tags? Do we have to label routes?

[03:37] Olivia Grant: You can. We also infer some from API features used—like if you’re using tool calls or JSON schema output. But the best results come from you labeling the route and giving a prompt set aligned to that.

[03:52] Jonas Weber: And the prompt set is key. Gating isn’t magic; it’s as good as the prompts and metrics you choose. We’re standardizing prompt-set storage and versioning so every gating decision references an immutable prompt-set revision.

[04:10] Tom Becker: If we don’t provide prompts, what happens?

[04:12] Jonas Weber: For pilot, we can start with Redwood baseline sets for generic chat and safety checks, but it will not catch domain-specific failures. For production gating, we strongly recommend “bring your own prompts” for your critical routes.

[04:28] Sarah Kim: What does “eval suite” mean here? Is it like a benchmark?

[04:33] Jonas Weber: It’s a set of tests with metrics. Example suite for support drafts might include: format adherence (did it follow the template), task success (did it answer the question), hallucination proxy checks (lightweight), and toxicity/safety. Some metrics are rubric-graded with a grader model; some are exact-match or schema validation.

[04:58] Anil Mehta: I’m worried about grader flakiness. We’ve seen LLM-as-judge be noisy.

[05:03] Jonas Weber: Yeah. Two things: we (1) enforce minimum sample sizes, and (2) use statistical guardrails—confidence intervals or “do not regress beyond X with high confidence.” The exact methodology can be tuned. For pilot, we usually start conservative to avoid false negatives, then tighten.

[05:26] Sarah Kim: Wait—false negatives meaning we miss a regression?

[05:28] Jonas Weber: Correct. False positives are “blocked even though it’s fine.” Both are bad, but in regulated customer-facing flows, you usually prefer fewer false negatives. We’ll tune based on your tolerance.

[05:45] Miguel Santos: Also, there’s staged rollout. During pilot we can run observe-only: do the evals, record results, but don’t block. That gives us baseline distributions.

[05:56] Tom Becker: That’s attractive. Because we can’t afford to have engineering blocked constantly.

[06:01] Ethan Park: Observe-only is literally a policy mode. Same plumbing, no enforcement. Then soft-block (requires override), then hard-block.

[06:15] Rachel Owens: Overrides. Who can override?

[06:18] Ethan Park: RBAC-based. Typically an “Optimize Admin” or “Platform Oncall” role. We can also require justification text and optionally a second approver depending on your setup.

[06:33] Rachel Owens: Second approver would be ideal for us.

[06:36] Ethan Park: Noted. We can confirm what’s supported in the first pilot scope.

[06:42] Olivia Grant: Let’s go into what “pass/fail” looks like in the UI. You’ll see a gating result panel: overall decision plus per-metric deltas. For example: task success -0.8%, format adherence -3.2% with confidence interval, safety unchanged. If it fails, it lists the metric and threshold violated, plus a link to artifacts and the eval run ID.

[07:06] Sarah Kim: Artifacts meaning the prompts and outputs?

[07:09] Olivia Grant: Depending on your retention settings and PII handling. We can store redacted outputs, or store only summaries. Many enterprise customers choose to keep full artifacts for a short window and then purge.

[07:22] Rachel Owens: We’ll need to talk about retention. Our support content can contain PII.

[07:27] Miguel Santos: Yep. We’ll pull in our security packet. But high level: encryption at rest, access controls, and configurable retention for eval artifacts.

[07:40] Anil Mehta: Timeouts—what if gating takes ten minutes?

[07:43] Olivia Grant: Great question. The eval run is async. The apply request goes into a “pending” state while the job runs. You can poll or the Console updates. We set timeouts and retry policies. For most suites we aim for a couple minutes; larger suites obviously longer.

[08:03] Ethan Park: And failure mode is explicit. If the eval runner is degraded, we can: block applies, or in some tiers allow manual approval. That’s a policy setting, not an ad hoc behavior.

[08:17] Sarah Kim: For us, we’d want: block by default, but allow emergency override with audit, because incidents happen.

[08:24] Rachel Owens: With the second approver.

[08:27] Ethan Park: Understood.

[08:30] Jonas Weber: On the methodology: for quantization changes, we usually require stricter suites. Because we’ve seen model-family-specific regressions—like structured output dropping a field, or tool args becoming invalid JSON.

[08:46] Tom Becker: That one is painful. Our downstream parser just breaks.

[08:50] Jonas Weber: Exactly. So we include schema validation metrics and “format adherence” as a first-class gate. In addition, we recommend a small set of “sentinel prompts” that are known to be brittle.

[09:05] Anil Mehta: Do you have examples?

[09:07] Jonas Weber: Common ones: multi-step instructions with strict bullet formatting, or tool-call with nested JSON arguments. We have generic ones, but we’d want you to contribute 10–20 of your own that represent failure modes you’ve seen.

[09:25] Sarah Kim: That’s doable. We can pull from incident retros.

[09:29] Miguel Santos: If it helps, we can set up a redaction workflow so you can share without customer identifiers.

[09:36] Sarah Kim: Good.

[09:39] Olivia Grant: Can I ask about your current stack? Are you on our hosted API now, or dedicated?

[09:44] Sarah Kim: We’re on dedicated capacity for the support draft route, and hosted for internal tools. We’re evaluating moving more to dedicated if we can get stable costs.

[09:54] Olivia Grant: Cool. The gating approach works the same across those. It’s control plane enforced, so it doesn’t matter if runtime is in dedicated pool.

[10:05] Anil Mehta: If we pin model versions, does gating also pin to that exact version?

[10:09] Ethan Park: Yes. A gating run references the exact model build identifier, plus your route config, plus prompt-set revision. If any of those change, cached eval results don’t apply.

[10:22] Anil Mehta: Cached eval results?

[10:24] Ethan Park: We cache eval summaries keyed on (model version, prompt-set rev, suite, config delta). So you don’t rerun identical things.

[10:35] Sarah Kim: That’s important for us cost-wise. Running huge evals every time is expensive.

[10:39] Jonas Weber: And it’s also about determinism. If you rerun constantly, you get drift from graders. Caching keeps “the decision used at time of apply” consistent.

[10:53] Rachel Owens: But then how do you handle if you discover a grader bug?

[10:56] Jonas Weber: Good question. That’s why suite versions are part of the key. If we bump the suite version because methodology changes, it invalidates old cache and you can re-evaluate.

[11:10] Sarah Kim: Let’s talk thresholds. Like, what is a typical threshold? We need a practical answer.

[11:16] Jonas Weber: Sure. For a “task success” metric scored 0–1, you might set “no more than -1% absolute regression” at 95% confidence, with minimum N=200 samples. For format adherence, you might set it tighter, like “no regression allowed” because a small drop can be catastrophic.

[11:39] Tom Becker: Yeah, any format break is a production incident.

[11:42] Jonas Weber: Exactly. Then for toxicity/safety, you can set absolute ceilings rather than deltas.

[11:52] Anil Mehta: Are these per-route? Because support drafts is different than policy Q&A.

[11:56] Jonas Weber: Per-workload type and optionally per-route. The schema supports overriding by tenant, route, model family.

[12:07] Ethan Park: From a system standpoint, policies are versioned documents. So you can say “Policy v3 is enforced for route X,” and we keep the history.

[12:18] Rachel Owens: That’s good for audits.

[12:20] Ethan Park: Exactly.

[12:23] Olivia Grant: Can we ask what “success” looks like for your pilot? Like, what would make you say yes to turning on hard-block.

[12:30] Sarah Kim: We want to see that it catches the regressions we care about. Specifically quantization changes that break structured output or increase hallucinations in policy responses. Also we want low operational overhead.

[12:44] Tom Becker: And we want a clean story for support: if something is blocked, the UI should explain it in English.

[12:51] Olivia Grant: Yep. The Console states we support are: pass, fail, timeout/degraded, and “override requested/approved.” We’re workshopping copy for those.

[13:05] Sarah Kim: Timeouts—what do you show? Because “timeout” sounds like your system is broken.

[13:11] Ethan Park: That’s fair. We can phrase it as “Evaluation not completed within SLA.” And we provide next actions: retry, inspect runner status, or request override depending on your permissions.

[13:25] Jonas Weber: Also, we can design suites so the gating suite is fast. You can run deeper nightly evals separately.

[13:33] Anil Mehta: Like a canary suite.

[13:34] Jonas Weber: Exactly. Lightweight gating suite for “apply-time,” deeper suite for monitoring and regression tracking.

[13:46] Miguel Santos: That also helps with deployment velocity. You don’t want a 2-hour benchmark gating every small change.

[13:54] Sarah Kim: Understood.

[14:00] Olivia Grant: On optimization types: would you be okay scoping pilot to quantization + routing, and leave batching/caching for phase 2?

[14:08] Sarah Kim: Maybe. Batching changes can also change latency spikes which impacts us, but quality-wise it’s less risky. I’d prioritize quant.

[14:19] Tom Becker: Same.

[14:21] Jonas Weber: Quant is where we’ve built the most specific guardrails anyway.

[14:26] Anil Mehta: How do you handle routing changes? Like fallback to another model.

[14:30] Olivia Grant: For routing, we treat it similarly: the “candidate config” means different model target or different fallback chain. The suite runs on the candidate target model, compare to baseline.

[14:45] Anil Mehta: And do you do A/B or canary in production?

[14:48] Ethan Park: That’s part of rollout policy. We can enforce gating before rollout. Then you can do canary traffic with monitoring. The guardrails are about blocking obviously risky changes before they hit users.

[15:05] Sarah Kim: Okay. Switching gears: what data do you need from us to start?

[15:10] Miguel Santos: We’ll need: (1) which routes you want in pilot, (2) representative prompt sets, and (3) what metrics matter. Jonas can help map metrics.

[15:22] Jonas Weber: If you can share 50–100 prompts per route, that’s enough to start observe-only. More is better for stats, but we can iterate.

[15:34] Sarah Kim: We can do 100 for support drafts, 50 for policy Q&A. But we’ll need redaction.

[15:41] Rachel Owens: And we need your retention story in writing.

[15:44] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[15:47] Olivia Grant: Minor note: structured output—are you using JSON schema mode or just “please output JSON” prompts?

[15:54] Tom Becker: We’re using JSON schema on the support drafts. On policy Q&A it’s mostly text plus citations.

[16:01] Olivia Grant: Great. That makes format adherence measurable.

[16:07] Jonas Weber: For citations, we can measure “citation presence” and consistency, but factuality is harder. We can use proxies: answer consistency, contradiction checks, or curated gold answers.

[16:22] Anil Mehta: We have some gold answers from compliance.

[16:25] Jonas Weber: That’s perfect. Even 20–30 gold items help.

[16:30] Sarah Kim: I want to understand: when you say “gating blocks apply,” is that only for Optimize-initiated changes, or any config change?

[16:38] Ethan Park: The project scope is Optimize-driven apply flow. If your engineers push a config change directly, that’s separate—though we can extend guardrails later.

[16:49] Sarah Kim: Got it.

[16:51] Rachel Owens: From governance perspective, we’d eventually want it for any change.

[16:55] Ethan Park: We’ve heard that. But for now, Optimize is the first enforcement point because it’s where automated cost changes happen.

[17:06] Olivia Grant: Let’s talk about real failure cases you’ve seen—so we ensure the suite catches them.

[17:11] Tom Becker: We had one where it started returning a slightly different JSON field name, like “finalAnswer” instead of “final_answer.” That broke everything.

[17:20] Jonas Weber: Great example. That’s a strict schema validation fail. We can gate on that with zero tolerance.

[17:28] Anil Mehta: Another is it stopped calling the tool in some edge cases. We do tool calling for account lookup.

[17:35] Olivia Grant: Are you using our tool-calling interface or something custom?

[17:38] Anil Mehta: Your tool calling. It sometimes… like, it returns a string describing the call instead of the call.

[17:45] Jonas Weber: That’s another known quantization failure mode: “tool-call compliance” drops. We can track tool call rate and argument validity.

[17:58] Sarah Kim: Good.

[18:00] Ethan Park: Also from enforcement: we can require additional suites for quant changes. Like if optimization_type=quantization, mandatory suites include structured-output compliance and tool-call compliance.

[18:13] Sarah Kim: Perfect.

[18:16] Rachel Owens: How do you prevent people from just overriding everything?

[18:20] Ethan Park: (1) RBAC: only certain roles. (2) Rate limits: you can cap overrides. (3) Audit: every override is logged with justification and approver, which tends to discourage abuse.

[18:37] Miguel Santos: And we can set it so overrides are disabled entirely if you want.

[18:41] Sarah Kim: We probably need overrides for incident response, but it should be rare.

[18:46] Jonas Weber: One thing we’ve done with others is “override requires a rerun” or “override requires a smaller safe suite to pass.” Not sure if that’s in phase one but conceptually.

[18:58] Ethan Park: We’re discussing that internally—like a “manual approval” state rather than a pure bypass.

[19:06] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[19:09] Olivia Grant: Latency impact: gating doesn’t add latency to your production requests; it only affects apply-time. But it does consume compute for evals.

[19:20] Anil Mehta: Where do evals run? On the same cluster as production?

[19:24] Olivia Grant: We isolate eval traffic. Dedicated environments can run evals in separate capacity pools so they don’t steal from production.

[19:34] Sarah Kim: Good.

[19:37] Jonas Weber: Another detail: we prefer deterministic settings for eval runs—temperature pinned, seed where applicable, and consistent decoding. Otherwise you’re gating on noise.

[19:49] Anil Mehta: Do you support seed?

[19:51] Olivia Grant: For some backends yes, but not universally. We’ll at least pin decoding parameters.

[19:58] Sarah Kim: Fine.

[20:01] Rachel Owens: Audit logs again: do they include the prompt content?

[20:05] Ethan Park: The audit event includes references: eval_run_id, suite_id, prompt_set_revision. It does not need to include raw prompts. That’s configurable and generally we keep the audit payload minimal for PII reasons.

[20:23] Rachel Owens: Great.

[20:25] Miguel Santos: We’re at about 20 minutes. Maybe shift to pilot timeline?

[20:30] Sarah Kim: Yes, what’s realistic?

[20:33] Miguel Santos: If you can share prompts in the next ~2 weeks, we can do an observe-only phase quickly. Then soft-block. Hard-block after we’re confident thresholds aren’t too noisy.

[20:45] Jonas Weber: Threshold tuning typically needs at least one iteration cycle. We look at distribution, false positive rate, adjust.

[20:54] Tom Becker: How will we see results? Dashboard?

[20:57] Olivia Grant: In Console, plus we have a dashboard for gating pass rate, fail reasons, eval latency, and override usage.

[21:07] Tom Becker: We’d want exports too.

[21:09] Ethan Park: Yep.

[21:12] Anil Mehta: Can we run our own eval harness? Like, use your runner but bring our eval code?

[21:18] Jonas Weber: The project is extending an existing harness. We can support custom metrics in some cases, but for pilot we should stick to standardized metrics so gating is stable.

[21:30] Sarah Kim: Understood.

[21:32] Olivia Grant: One more technical question: do you have multiple regions? Data residency constraints?

[21:37] Rachel Owens: Mostly US. No strict EU residency today.

[21:42] Olivia Grant: Okay.

[21:45] Sarah Kim: I want to drill into “confidence intervals” a bit. Are you actually doing stats tests or is it like heuristics?

[21:53] Jonas Weber: In the current design, we compute metric deltas and confidence bounds based on sample size and variance. Some metrics are binomial (pass/fail), some continuous. For pilot we can start with a conservative approach: require a minimum N and require the lower bound of candidate to be within threshold.

[22:15] Anil Mehta: That sounds reasonable.

[22:18] Jonas Weber: We also handle “flaky” graders by rerunning a subset if variance is too high.

[22:27] Sarah Kim: Doesn’t that increase cost?

[22:30] Jonas Weber: Slightly, but only when results are borderline.

[22:34] Ethan Park: And from a policy engine perspective, we codify these rules so decisions are deterministic given the eval summary.

[22:43] Rachel Owens: Deterministic is good. We can’t have “it passed yesterday and failed today” with same inputs.

[22:49] Jonas Weber: Exactly why we version everything.

[22:53] Olivia Grant: Another thing: gating results show “baseline” vs “candidate.” Baseline is your currently running config.

[23:00] Sarah Kim: What if baseline is already bad?

[23:02] Jonas Weber: Great point. In that case, gating based on “no regression” doesn’t help. We can also support “absolute thresholds” (“must be above 0.85 task success”) not just deltas.

[23:16] Sarah Kim: For us, we’d want both.

[23:19] Jonas Weber: Makes sense.

[23:22] Tom Becker: How about rollback? If something passes and then we see production issues.

[23:27] Ethan Park: The apply records are tied into rollback hooks. You can revert to previous config, and we can also have automatic fallback policies if you have them enabled.

[23:38] Olivia Grant: Plus monitoring. Guardrails doesn’t replace production monitoring; it reduces risk.

[23:45] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[23:47] Miguel Santos: Let’s do a quick recap of what we need from Acme. Sarah, you said you can share 100 prompts for support drafts, 50 for policy Q&A, plus some gold answers.

[24:00] Sarah Kim: Yes. We’ll work on redaction. We can also share examples of tool-call failures.

[24:07] Miguel Santos: Great.

[24:09] Rachel Owens: And from our side, we need: SOC 2, data retention details, and whether overrides can be 2-person.

[24:17] Ethan Park: We’ll respond.

[24:20] Olivia Grant: We’ll also send the technical doc that describes the gating output format, and the suite selection logic by optimization type.

[24:28] Jonas Weber: And I’ll propose initial thresholds—like strict schema adherence zero tolerance, plus task success delta bounds.

[24:36] Sarah Kim: Perfect.

[24:38] (crosstalk)

[24:39] Tom Becker: One last question: If Optimize recommends a change, can we see “why it thinks cost will improve” and “why it might harm quality” together?

[24:49] Olivia Grant: In the Console we show expected cost/latency impact, and the gating section shows quality risk evaluation. They’re adjacent in the apply panel.

[25:01] Tom Becker: Good.

[25:03] Anil Mehta: And can we run gating without applying? Like, evaluate a proposed change before we commit.

[25:09] Ethan Park: Yes, there’s an API path conceptually like “propose → run gating → decide apply.” In UI, you basically get that because apply is pending until gating completes.

[25:21] Sarah Kim: Great.

[25:23] Miguel Santos: I think we’ve covered most of it. Anything else from your side?

[25:28] Rachel Owens: Just a note: we’ll want an audit log example that a compliance person can read.

[25:33] Ethan Park: We’ll include sample events and field definitions.

[25:37] Sarah Kim: And timeline: let’s schedule kickoff next week.

[25:41] Miguel Santos: Done. I’ll send times.

[25:44] Olivia Grant: Thanks all.

---

(Recording continues with light scheduling discussion and side questions; transcript quality drops slightly.)

[26:02] Speaker 2: Uh, can you do Tuesday morning?

[26:05] Miguel Santos: Tuesday 10 Pacific maybe? I’ll email options.

[26:10] Sarah Kim: Works.

[26:12] Anil Mehta: Also, do you support running this in our VPC later?

[26:17] Olivia Grant: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC deployment. Guardrails control plane can be private as well, but we can scope that separately.

[26:28] Sarah Kim: Okay, not in pilot.

[26:30] Miguel Santos: Cool. We’ll wrap. Thanks everyone.

(End)
